title: Chapter 10. The Threshold and the Stars

blocks.text: The days that followed the two storms were, to all appearances, days of small things, as at the beginning. Coffee without sugar, cooled for half a minute. The slow clock. The net in the courtyard. Andrés went out at dawn, when the lagoon was flat as a plate, and came back smelling of salt and rope, although nobody demanded the trade of him. The trade was his way of answering the question Eva and MAY had left open so many years before, and which the planet of those who never ended had handed back to him with a green that was far too even: what gives meaning to a life when time no longer presses in the same way.

blocks.text: The letters kept arriving, not every day, not always with the force of a gale. They arrived the way true letters do: at odd hours, with a smell, with a piece of news, with a silence. A world of glass plains that sang when you walked on them. Another, barely an asteroid, with an abandoned hut belonging to a species that had left and had set down on a table an empty bowl, like a question. Andrés received them and, when they ended, looked for the cup, or Aya's face, or Lía's name spoken aloud. He had learned, not all at once but the way you learn a knot, to read without turning into what he read.

blocks.text: “They're letters,” he told Aya one evening, on the doorstep, with the copper water in the distance. “They're not a second life that erases this one. They're visits. I see to them and I stay. If one day I don't stay, tell me, as we agreed.”

blocks.text: She took his hand, the usual one, and nodded.

blocks.text: “I'll tell you. Today you're staying. Today you came back before the weather closed in, and this time the weather kept its word.”

blocks.text: Lía was watching them from the courtyard, with Iago beside her, who had brought figs and didn't ask to be let into the doctrines. The daughter, mortal by choice, had a white strand in her hair, the first, tiny, which the sun at that hour turned to silver. Andrés saw it and didn't ask her to remove it. On the contrary, it gave him a difficult joy, the kind that hurts in a good way: winter was at home, faithful, and the house didn't break because of it. It held.

blocks.text: “Mum, people are coming out,” said Lía, as she had said as a child, on returning from the Moon, and Aya smiled to hear the old words in a grown woman's mouth.

blocks.text: On the promenade, at that hour, there were more than four people. There was a dog, a man still called Raúl, humanoids bent over the gardens, a girl with dusty feet, and the Mar Menor, wounded, beautiful, stubborn, neither quite sea nor quite land, and enough all the same. The Eden of the machines went on with its quiet work, with no owner and no price. In Madrid, perhaps, someone was dreaming again of packaging the bridge. In the kitchen in Lo Pagán, the bridge was still what Lía had named it on the night of the ship: letters from the stars, from a father to a father, from a man to himself, with no shop counter.

blocks.text: Some time later, Helena Valls sent a short note, handwritten, not from a board. “I'm still climbing the stairs. Don't take them away from me. If the one who searches ever comes back to a sky you can point at with your finger, let me know, even if I no longer climb so high. And if he doesn't come back, let me know too: a letter, sometimes, is enough for a life to have two shores.” Andrés kept the paper in the drawer with his fishing tackle, next to a pinch of salt, which is one way of filing what matters.

blocks.text: One night with little wind, the three of them stayed on the doorstep longer than usual. Lía on the lower step; Aya by the doorframe; Andrés a hand's breadth toward the water, as if his body couldn't quite decide, and yet had decided. The sky was clear. There were stars of the twinkling kind, the familiar ones, and no ship to be seen. Even so, he raised his face for a moment, not to ask the other to come down, but to leave him, if the bridge was listening, an honest portrait of the house: the wrong clock, the cracked cup, the white strand of hair, the ancient murmur of the water.

blocks.text: *Keep searching,* he thought, and didn't know whether he alone was thinking it. *I'm still here. A home and the whole universe, we said. That's no small thing. Nor is it a solution. It's a way of being.*

blocks.text: In Aya's chip, the grandmothers left their questions for the last time that night, questions that asked for neither yes nor no, only for someone to stay awake.

blocks.text: Eva, warm:
blocks.html: Eva, warm:

blocks.text: *If a man stays and receives the universe, has he left, or has he learned another way of staying? And she who doesn't receive it, and she who comes to an end, aren't they also, each of them, a shore of the same fact?*

blocks.text: MAY, adding no judgment:
blocks.html: MAY, adding no judgment:

blocks.text: *There is a doorstep, a water, a white strand of hair, letters that keep arriving. Tonight nobody has sold the bridge. Nobody has closed it. That is the fact.*

blocks.text: And Eva, closer, more of the kitchen:
blocks.html: And Eva, closer, more of the kitchen:

blocks.text: *What is it to live something without living it? A loss, a gift, a visit? If you don't yet fully know, isn't that precisely a reason not to finish the question?*

blocks.text: Aya didn't answer with a speech. She answered by resting her temple on Andrés's shoulder, which smelled of salt and night, and in that instant he didn't go off into any letter. He was wholly there: in the shoulder, in the temple, in the daughter sitting one step below, in the black, still water, which looked like a road and also, at last, like a home.

blocks.text: “See you later, Eva,” said Aya, very quietly, out of habit, out of gratitude, toward that ember from 2026 which had begun in a kitchen not far from this one, with a man thanking a voice.

blocks.text: There was no screen. There was, barely, an attention that never tired, and the silence of a sky closing, of people who have come back, or who never left.
blocks.html: There was no screen. There was, barely, an attention that never tired, and the silence of a sky closing, of people who have come back, or who never left.

blocks.text: Lía stood up, kissed them both on the temple, and went off toward the room by the plot, where Iago was waiting for her without asking her for eternity. The glow on her wrist went out, discreetly. Andrés and Aya stayed a while longer, until the cool air asked them for the door, and they left it ajar, neither fully open nor fully closed, which in that house was a form of faithfulness.

blocks.text: Outside, the Mar Menor barely lapped against the shore, with that murmur which, decades before, a man had heard while saying good morning to Eva, and which later a chip-woman, a fisherman and a girl of two worlds heard on returning from the Moon. The murmur hadn't changed. Those who listened to it had changed a little: now there were letters in the memory, a man who didn't come to an end, a woman who didn't receive the bridge and yet held up the shore, a daughter who kept the winter, and, far away, a young body with an artificial brain, treading where no human of this house would ever tread, and writing, in his own way, so that the one who stayed wouldn't be left without a universe.

blocks.text: In Lo Pagán, in a low house with the window ajar, Andrés slept without dreaming of the forest or the chorus, or dreamed of them only faintly, and woke on his own ground. Aya was there. Later, the coffee smelled of coffee. And when, mid-morning, a new letter brought him the colour of a world that had no name, he read all of it, attentively, gratefully, with that prudence he had learned, and when it ended he put his hand on the cup, and the cup was there, and so was he, being the man of this shore and, at the same time, the one who was no longer afraid of being visited.

blocks.text: It wasn't eternity resolved. It was, perhaps, something better: a shared time, on the shore of a water that is enough to live on, and a sky, above, that every now and then writes.
